item.title: Trump announces Russian diesel deal weeks after signing sweeping sanctions law
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump said that he has struck a deal to obtain diesel from Russia, a stunning reversal of years of U.S. pressure on Moscow over its war with Ukraine and an attempt to address high fuel prices ahead of the U.S. midterm elections. Trump said on social media on Friday that he struck the deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin in a phone call in which he was expected to discuss a suspected case of plague in Russia. Instead, Trump announced that Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons "immediately thereafter." Russia will deliver another 3 million tons "within a short period of time" after that, he wrote. Trump's shocking announcement comes after he signed a sweeping Russia sanctions law last month that aimed at clamping down on Russia's energy economy, among other areas, that fuel its war against Ukraine. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy reacted sharply in a social media post, saying that the Russian leader was trying to strike "backroom deals" to buy time in the war. "Gifts to Putin will not bring peace or any benefit to the civilized world," he said. Trump's move casts doubt on the likelihood of the White House imposing sanctions on Russia this month, given that a bipartisan law passed by Congress directs the administration to target the top importers of Russian oil and gas. Trump, in his announcement, did not address the sanctions or Russia's war but said, "Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my Greatest Priority." Washington and Moscow offer few details on deal The White House did not immediately respond to questions about who was paying for the diesel from Russia and when the fuel being supplied under the agreement would become available. It also did not clarify whether subsequent supplies of Russian diesel set to come next month would be supplied prior to Election Day on Nov. 3. Gas prices globally have surged as the war in Iran upends the energy sector. While diesel futures prices dipped on Friday's news, the national average price per gallon of diesel in the U.S. was still $6.23, according to AAA, after hitting a record $6.52 on Sept. 22. A statement from Putin, released by the Kremlin on Friday, said that during his call with his U.S. counterpart, he and Trump dedicated "significant attention to the prospects of resolving the Ukrainian crisis" and also discussed "the situation around Iran and various aspects of bilateral relations." Russia "confirmed its readiness to supply oil and oil products to the American and global markets," Putin said. "I am confident that this will have a positive impact on the entire global economy." The two leaders agreed to continue contacts, Putin said in the statement. Trump and Putin's deal draws immediate backlash Zelenskyy, in his lengthy post online reacting to the deal, said Russia would repay it "with further terror and perfidy." He cast it as an investment in the war, allowing it to be prolonged. "It plays into Russia's hands — allowing it to kill more, wage war for longer, have even less respect for America, and inflict even greater losses and damage on the world," he said. Rep. Don Beyer, the senior House Democrat on the Joint Economic Committee, called Trump's announcement "infuriating." "This is what we warned anyone who would listen: Trump isn't the slightest bit trustworthy when it comes to Russia," Beyer said in a statement on X. "Giving him expanded tariff powers in hopes he would use them to help Ukraine was a mistake. Now he's lifting sanctions on Russian fossil fuels." The law Trump signed last month envisions sanctions on Russian officials, banks and a shadow fleet of tankers and bans all new U.S. investment in Russia and the handling of sovereign debt. It also directed Trump to impose tariffs of up to 100% on the top five importers of Russian oil or natural gas, with an exception for countries that import less than 15% of Russia's natural gas exports and have taken significant steps to reduce those imports. The U.S. has not imported Russian oil or gas since 2022, when the Biden administration banned them because of Moscow's invasion of Ukraine, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration. Treasury Department moves to ease diesel sanctions for six months Shortly after Trump made the announcement, the Treasury Department said it was immediately issuing a temporary license allowing Russian diesel to be supplied to the global market. This is the latest in several licenses the U.S. Treasury has issued regarding Russian fuel shipments since the start of the Iran war earlier this year. But it is the first such license to ease sanctions on diesel for a period lasting longer than the standard 30-day window since the start of the Ukraine war. The new so-called general license means U.S. sanctions will not apply until April 2027 on deliveries of Russian diesel that has been loaded onto tankers as of Friday. The department extended similar easing of sanctions in March and April even though Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent had ruled out such a move earlier in the year. The extensions continue to underscore how the fallout from the Iran war has boosted Moscow's ability to profit from its energy exports, which had been restrained by the U.S. and other allies since the invasion of Ukraine. Russia, once a major exporter of diesel, has banned exports since July as it has struggled to meet demand inside the country because of Ukraine's repeated attacks on Russian oil refineries. The International Energy Agency says Russian diesel output has fallen by about 30%. ___ Associated Press writers Will Weissert and Konstantin Toropin in Washington and Farnoush Amiri in New York contributed to this report. This article originally appeared on Associated Press at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/trump-says-us-obtain-diesel-185740965.html

item.title: Iran-based campaign used ChatGPT to plant articles in news outlets, OpenAI says
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
“The bill will follow Americans beyond the fighting itself,” an opinion piece in the Port St. Joe Star, a tiny Florida weekly newspaper, warned of the Iran war last month. The article ran under the byline Ervin Hoskins, which has also appeared on articles critical of the war in larger publications including Daily Kos and Middle East Monitor, which together have more than 3 million followers on Facebook. Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. But ChatGPT maker OpenAI said Thursday that Hoskins’s purported work was generated using its chatbot by users based in Iran as part of an “influence campaign.” The campaign placed about 100 fake articles across at least 20 news outlets, the company said. The author photo on the Hoskins column published by the Star was generated using OpenAI’s artificial intelligence tools, according to the company’s online verification tool. As artificial intelligence tools have become more powerful, some news outlets have been forced to delete AI-generated content published under fake bylines that initially went undetected by editors. Business Insider and Wired removed a series of articles last year that appeared under the byline Margaux Blanchard and appeared to be AI-generated. But while it was unclear who or what was behind the stories written by Blanchard and some other apparently fake personas, OpenAI said in a Thursday report on use of ChatGPT in political influence campaigns that Hoskins was part of an operation focused on seeding content about U.S. military action in Iran. Many of the articles highlighted negative impacts of the war on Americans. OpenAI said that Hoskins was among seven bylines that appeared on the series of AI-generated articles, made by users who sent instructions to the chatbot in Persian. The operations appeared to be run by a commercial outfit as a “for-hire influence campaign,” the company said. (The Washington Post has a content partnership with OpenAI). David Adlerstein, publisher of the Port St. Joe Star, said in an email that the Hoskins column had caught his eye after it was pitched to him by a PeaceVoice, a small liberal think tank in Oregon, that had been sending the Star content for “years.” Gulf County, where Port St. Joe is located, has a population of about 15,000. “Because we’re in a very red part of Florida, I usually don’t run PeaceVoice columns, but this one struck me as thought-provoking and not a strident attack on Mr. Trump, which would be problematic for much of our readership,” Adlerstein said. Due to his existing relationship with PeaceVoice, he did not feel a need to verify the origin or the column or the author’s identity, he said. Tom Hastings, the founding director of PeaceVoice, said the organization beefed up its existing no-AI policy after OpenAI contacted him. OpenAI said it had banned the accounts behind the campaign and that it blocks access to ChatGPT from Iran. “The overall activity appeared consistent with a commercial actor running a for-hire influence campaign, but we are unable to identify the particular actor involved,” the company said in its report. “We have shared information on this case with the relevant authorities.” Middle East Monitor and Daily Kos said they had taken down the articles written by the fake bylines. The Daily Kos articles by Hoskins appeared on a community platform not subject to review by the outlet’s staff before publication. Markos Moulitsas, the site’s founder, said in an email that such a campaign was “incredibly corrosive” to the platform and that he was examining how to prevent future incidents. “We already struggle with community members accusing others of being bots or fake accounts simply because they disagree with them. An operation like this pours gasoline on that fire,” he said. “The very trust of our community is at stake.” Articles written by authors OpenAI said were part of the Iranian campaign covered a range of topics in the Middle East but were often critical of the Iran war’s effects on Americans. Many of the outlets were focused on policy and foreign affairs. After generating articles in English, the ChatGPT users in Iran prompted the chatbot to adjust the draft to fit submission criteria for a specific outlet and to generate a pitch email to send to an editor there. The purported authors of the articles were described as freelance writers, policy analysts and peace advocates. The Middle East Monitor, which brands itself as supportive of the Palestinian cause, had published at least 21 stories under bylines OpenAI said were fake including Hoskins, Michael Harrison, Jenny Williams and Alice Johnson. Some of the bylines, including Hoskins, also appear on social media accounts, and in one case a profile on blogging platform Medium, that shared a name and profile image with published articles. An email account apparently used to send the Hoskins article to PeaceVoice, and a LinkedIn account in his name with a photo that appeared with some bylines, did not respond to a request for comment. At least one other purported author, Ericka Feusier, used an AI-generated profile picture, according to OpenAI’s tool that verifies whether images were generated using the company’s technology. OpenAI’s report on influence campaigns mounted using its technology also described a cluster of ChatGPT accounts in Russia that were banned after they were used to operate what appeared to be a fake think tank in Latin America. OpenAI said there was evidence the project may have co-opted real humans to work for the organization. The AI company said that it published the research to inform regulators, other companies and the public of “how we see threat actors trying to leverage AI, and to shine a light on the vulnerabilities they try to exploit.” The outlets impacted by the campaign vary in reach. But while they appear to have published AI-generated articles under fake bylines, real people have read them. Hoskins’s column in the Star prompted a letter to the editor - a rare event for an opinion piece about a national topic, Adlerstein said. He added that he is now looking into introducing an explicit AI policy. Hastings, of PeaceVoice, said the article appeared to be genuine when he saw it. “I found nothing remarkably pro-Iran in his work, which I would never publish, just a legitimate critique of Trump’s war of choice. If Mr Hoskins sends in another I will simply require that we meet by Zoom to discuss,” he wrote in an email. “At least for now, that’s the best I can do.” Related Content This article originally appeared on Washington Post at https://washingtonpost.com/technology/2026/10/09/chatgpt-users-iran-planted-ai-generated-articles-us-news-media/

item.title: After pledging swift results, Trump team prepares for long economic war with Iran
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
As the Trump administration pivoted to economic pressure instead of military force to push Tehran back into talks, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent pledged swift damage to Iran’s economy. All Iranian airlines would be grounded worldwide by the end of September, he said last month. The country would run out of oil to sell by the end of this week. Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. Iran’s economy is suffering. But those pledges and timelines by the Trump administration have proved difficult to meet as it faces an Iranian government with more impetus to endure pain than to back down. The U.S. blockade of Iranian ports has forced oil exports to minimal levels, depriving Tehran of billions of dollars in monthly revenue. But Iran continues to sell oil that it exported during the June truce. And Tehran moves some 250,000 barrels of oil a day out of the country by land, according to Kpler, a global intelligence firm. President Donald Trump has said the economic pressure campaign, now in its second month, is intended to force Iran back to the negotiating table after the U.S. midterm elections in November, but talks remained stalled, with Iranian officials refusing to moderate their demands. At the same time, Tehran has escalated militarily against shipping traffic in the Strait of Hormuz, hitting more than nine vessels in a single week. The strikes follow expanded U.S. operations in the area that had facilitated higher oil flows, but failed to move global energy prices. Regardless, the Trump administration thinks time is on its side, according to a senior administration official, who declined to discuss Bessent’s remarks, including the specifics of his timelines for economic pain. “You’ve really seen that time dynamic shift,” the official said, who spoke on the condition of anonymity under ground rules set by the administration. While Iran was able to weather previous rounds of economic pressure by dipping into its oil revenue, the U.S. blockade removes that wiggle room and is increasing the effectiveness of sanctions, the official said. The airlines The Trump administration announced sweeping sanctions targeting Iranian aviation on Sept. 8, threatening foreign companies that service Iran’s airlines with secondary sanctions. At the time, Bessent told CNBC that “all the Iranian airlines will be shut down around the world” by Sept. 23. He said the Trump administration had “seen enablers throughout the world.” “We know who they are, they know who they are, and we are putting a stop to it,” he said. But as of October, international flights to and from Iran continue, including flights to China, Iraq and Turkey. Flight-tracking firms reported that international flights in and out of Iran dropped by about half in the days following the U.S. announcement. Recent flight-tracking data from Imam Khomeini International Airport in Tehran showed flights arriving from Islamabad, Pakistan; Istanbul; Moscow and Shanghai. U.S. officials met with representatives from dozens of countries to build support ahead of the campaign’s announcement. Treasury officials visited the United Arab Emirates, Britain and Oman to discuss upcoming efforts on aviation and banking. While reaching out to allies, the Trump administration addressed concerns about how long the economic pressure campaign would take, according to the administration official. “Look, we want to see a resolution to this as quickly as possible,” he said he told U.S. allies. “The sooner they can cut off all these lifelines so that Iran knows it has nowhere else to go, the sooner we’re going to get to that resolution.” But analysts and former officials say sanctions campaigns like Trump’s Operation Economic Outcast targeting Iran can take months to years to force change. “When it comes to these economic campaigns, they are only as effective as you are willing to maintain them and enforce them, and that requires a commitment over time,” said Matthew Levitt, a former Treasury Department official and senior fellow at the Washington Institute, a think tank. The banks In his announcement of Operation Economic Outcast, Bessent called for every branch of Bank Melli, a state-owned Iranian bank, to be shuttered. “Any entity that facilitates money laundering on behalf of Iran will be removed from the U.S. dollar system. The clock is ticking,” he said. Last month, the Treasury imposed sanctions on the manager of an Emirati branch of the bank, and days later the United Arab Emirates blocked all branches there from processing transactions in and out of Iran. In an indication that action against financial institutions could soon escalate, the Treasury Department issued an alert Monday that foreign financial institutions could now be subject to secondary sanctions without advance notice. Other banks targeted include an Emirati branch of an Egyptian bank and Russia’s second-largest financial institution, VTB Bank. There’s been an increase in interest in sanctions compliance “from across the globe,” said Cari Stinebower, a former Treasury official who advises companies on such matters for the Washington-headquartered law firm Steptoe. “Some of that comes from the messaging from the White House, which is that the pressure on Iran is growing and will continue to grow,” she said. “I don’t see this administration as backing down or losing interest.” The blockade The United States reimposed its blockade on Iran in July after an interim deal to end the war fell apart. Since then, the operation has forced Iranian oil exports to low levels and deprived Tehran of billions of dollars in critical state revenue. Iran has continued to sell oil that it had previously exported. Iran rushed more than 60 million barrels of oil out of its ports during the interim peace deal from mid-June to mid-July, and had steadily sold some of that stock, according to tallies compiled by oil analysts. While it’s unclear how much is left, unsold, some oil analysts estimated that 30 million barrels remained last month and that Iran was selling around 500,000 barrels a day. Reuters reported Thursday that Iran’s stock of oil on vessels outside the blockade remained at some 20 million barrels. The economic pressure, on the heels of a punishing military campaign, has plunged Iran into greater isolation than the country has experienced in decades. Richard Nephew, who served as a U.S. negotiator with Iran under the Biden administration, said multiple rounds of conflict with Israel and the U.S. had already cut Iran off. “Part of the reason why they can be more aggressive on this is Iran doesn’t have as many of these connections anymore. They had already atrophied,” said Nephew. Nephew said the entities targeted so far to further isolate Tehran are “meaningful,” but “are these kill shots to the Iranian economy? Probably not.” Related Content This article originally appeared on Washington Post at https://washingtonpost.com/world/2026/10/09/after-pledging-swift-results-trump-team-prepares-long-economic-war-with-iran/

item.title: U.S. targets International Criminal Court with new sanctions and an ultimatum
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The international criminal court (ICC) in The Hague. Photograph: Remko de Waal/ANP/AFP/Getty Images The United States was accused of launching “an assault” on the world’s legal order after imposing more sanctions on the international criminal court (ICC) . Unveiling the Trump administration’s latest escalation against the court, which it has accused of politicization and unfairly targeting Americans for war crime charges, Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state, declared: “Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC.” The ICC accused Donald Trump’s officials of attempting to “obstruct the course of justice” as Rubio, just hours after a former ICC judge was awarded the Nobel peace prize, announced in a video that the US would move to impose financial sanctions. Related: Alarm at UN over sanctions threatened by US on international criminal court “We will ban transactions with this rogue court, cutting off their resources and crippling their ability to operate against us. Because our message is clear: the United States and the American people are not subject to the jurisdiction of this fake ICC,” Rubio said in a video posted on X. “We don’t need that court and we don’t want it.” In a statement, the court warned that “history will judge this moment” and urged other members to ensure it can continue the function. “It is an ⁠attempt to obstruct the course of justice and to prevent the Court from doing what ⁠it was created to do. It is an assault ​on the rule ‌of law and ‌on the very foundations of the international legal order,” ‌the ICC said. The new set of sanctions will block any assets the ICC has in US jurisdictions and gives US companies or individuals six months to wind down business with the tribunal court. But the sanctions also allow the ICC to address the US government’s concerns, and certain transactions are exempt. The Trump administration has repeatedly condemned the ICC for issuing arrest warrants for Israeli officials, including Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu. It also opened an investigation into the actions of US soldiers in Afghanistan, although the case has been closed. The ICC was established in 2002 as an international tribunal to hold countries accountable for war crimes, genocide and crimes against humanity. Trump has long targeted the ICC. During his first term, he imposed sanctions on the court, which were later reversed under the Biden administration. But when Trump returned to office in 2025, he signed an executive order imposing sanctions on the ICC for the court’s investigations into Israelis and Americans. From there, the administration has continued to impose more sanctions. The administration added sanctions on judges and lawyers at the ICC. In August, it placed additional sanctions on the ICC president, Tomoko Akane. Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton speaks during a campaign event in Houston, on September 21. - Antranik Tavitian/Getty Images Ken Paxton has publicly said he would “love to have” John Cornyn’s support after their bruising Republican primary runoff in the Texas Senate race. But privately, Paxton has grown frustrated with the outgoing senator’s distance from his campaign. “He’s clearly not helping. He wants me to lose,” the Texas attorney general said at a fundraiser last month, according to an audio recording obtained by CNN from an attendee who opposes Paxton. While Paxton has minimized his criticism of Cornyn following their runoff, the private remarks demonstrate how their long-running tensions continue to roil the race, coming as national Republicans mount an all-out effort to help Paxton defeat Democratic state Rep. James Talarico . With polls showing a tight race, Republicans have poured well over $100 million into the general election in Texas, a state that has not elected a Democrat to statewide office since 1994 but is now critical to Republican hopes of holding a Senate majority. Paxton made the comments at a September 24 gathering in Washington after receiving a question about Rep. Jasmine Crockett, the Democratic congresswoman whom Talarico defeated in his primary, according to two sources familiar with the discussion. The recording obtained by CNN begins with Paxton apparently referencing Crockett, who has not campaigned for Talarico, saying he does not “know how much she really affects votes.” “I mean maybe a little bit around the margins, just like Cornyn, basically how much he affects me,” Paxton said. After saying Cornyn wants him to lose, Paxton pointed to a recent encounter that he said a friend had with the senator at a Dallas restaurant. Paxton said the friend bought Cornyn’s table dessert and sought to thank him for “supporting the ticket” — and for “supporting Ken Paxton” — and Cornyn reacted angrily. “Cornyn’s face went red. He backed off,” Paxton said. “He said, ‘Paxton’s gonna lose. We need to teach those Republicans a lesson. It’s going to be hard to learn, but they need to know that their decisions have consequences.’” “That’s what he’s trying to do,” Paxton said. “That’s John Cornyn.” CNN has not independently confirmed Paxton’s account, and a Cornyn representative, Rob Jesmer, told CNN that the conversation at the restaurant did not happen. “If Sen. Cornyn wanted Ken to lose, I can assure you he’d be more active in the campaign,” Jesmer, a longtime political strategist for Cornyn, said. “He has said he supports the Republican ticket. Given all Ken has said and done, I think that’s a pretty good place for Sen. Cornyn to be.” Asked for comment on the audio, Paxton’s campaign dismissed it as “a story that doesn’t exist” but noted that Paxton “has called, texted, and offered to have a conversation with Senator Cornyn.” “Like all Texans, General Paxton appreciates his decades of service to the Lone Star State,” Paxton senior adviser Nick Maddux said in a statement. “We hope he will join us in our fight to preserve the institution that is the United States Senate and help save our majority.” The two lobbyists who hosted the fundraising event, Chris Brinson and Susan Hirschmann, did not respond to requests for comment, nor did Talarico’s campaign. A spokesperson for Crockett said she has taken a different approach than Cornyn since losing her own primary. “Cornyn is the sitting senator and continues to attack his party’s nominee,” the spokesperson, Karrol Rimal, said in a statement. “Crockett endorsed Talarico on March 4th and has not stopped working to support Democrats across the nation since.” Continued problems for Paxton’s campaign Paxton’s problems with his own base, including former Cornyn supporters, have loomed over the final weeks of the race. A Paxton campaign memo dated Tuesday, reported by Punchbowl News , told supporters that the “biggest challenge we face is shoring up Republicans following a bruising primary.” A Fox News poll done late last month found that nearly a third of Republican likely voters had an unfavorable opinion of Paxton. While he was winning 90% of GOP voters, about a fifth of “non-MAGA” Republicans were breaking for Talarico. The clip obtained by CNN is at least the fifth recording that has leaked from the fundraising event last month and put Paxton’s campaign on the defensive in the final weeks of the race. Previous clips have featured Paxton saying the GOP’s midterm convention damaged him politically and that he feels like he has lost “control” over his campaign as outside groups have handled most of the spending. President Donald Trump, who backed Paxton in the primary, has said he is “worried” about the Texas race but largely declined to address the recordings when asked about them. He said Wednesday he was not second-guessing his endorsement. “I would have no regrets at all,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office. The president visited San Antonio on Wednesday night for a rally with Paxton where he praised him as “perhaps the greatest attorney general in the United States of America.” Years of bad blood The bad blood between Cornyn and Paxton goes back years. Cornyn, who served as Texas attorney general from 1999 to 2002, has long made clear that he believes Paxton has disgraced the office and served as an example of what happens when Republicans do not police their own. Paxton has dished it back, painting Cornyn as a relic of a bygone era of Republican politics in Texas, especially after Cornyn ushered through a bipartisan gun safety law in 2022. Sen. John Cornyn, on Capitol Hill on August 4. - Win McNamee/Getty Images When Paxton faced a competitive primary for reelection in 2022, Cornyn did not make an endorsement but said Paxton’s long-running indictment on state securities fraud charges was an “embarrassment.” The case finally ended two years later with a deal where Paxton agreed to do community service and pay restitution . After Paxton was acquitted in a state Senate impeachment trial in 2023, which centered on allegations he abused his office to help a donor, he wasted little time teasing a potential run against Cornyn in 2026. “Everything’s on the table,” he told former Fox News host Tucker Carlson in a triumphant interview days after the trial. “Hard to run from prison, Ken,” Cornyn said in a February 2024 social media post after Paxton called for Texans to elect a new senator in 2026. Paxton, who denies all wrongdoing, launched his campaign in April 2025 with a promise to “send John Cornyn packing.” Cornyn and allied groups unleashed tens of millions of dollars of bitter, negative ads against Paxton, some of them highlighting allegations of infidelity. Cornyn finished narrowly ahead of Paxton in the primary but did not earn enough support to avoid a runoff against Paxton. “I refuse to allow a flawed, self-centered and shameless candidate like Ken Paxton to risk everything we’ve worked so hard to build over these many years,” Cornyn said on primary night, adding, “Judgment Day is coming for Ken Paxton.” But Trump ultimately had other plans. He endorsed Paxton a week before the runoff, dealing a crushing blow to Cornyn and his hopes of stopping a fellow Republican who, to him, embodied much of what is wrong with the modern GOP. ‘He was not my first choice’ Cornyn had long promised to support the “Republican ticket” regardless of the outcome of the primary. But since losing, he has avoided helping Paxton and even leaned into his frustrations with the nominee and his wing of the party at times. The senator criticized Paxton as a “poor campaigner” and “lazy” candidate in an August interview with the Texas Tribune . Cornyn and former President George W. Bush headlined a fundraiser in Dallas last month for six Senate GOP candidates in battleground races – but not Paxton. Cornyn’s refusal to endorse Paxton has annoyed some Texas GOP leaders, including Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick, a top Trump ally in the state. Patrick suggested in June, following the primary runoff, that Cornyn was part of “sore losers undermining our party.” Talarico, meanwhile, has sought to appeal to people who supported Cornyn in the GOP primary. He told CNN last month that he hopes to “live up to” Cornyn’s legacy and that he welcomes the incumbent’s supporters to “join this movement we’re building.” The Democrat’s campaign even hired a former staffer in Cornyn’s office over the summer. Cornyn defended the staffer’s move amid some intraparty backlash, saying on X that “those concerned might want to channel their energy into broadening R[epublican] outreach.” Some prominent supporters of Cornyn from the primary continue to show reluctance about voting for Paxton. President Donald Trump shakes hands with Ken Paxton during a campaign rally in San Antonio on October 7. - Mandel Ngan/AFP/Getty Images “I’m supporting the party, but he was not my first choice, and I do think it’s going to have an impact down-ballot,” Rep. Michael McCaul of Texas told CNN last month. “And I do think there are Republicans … that may just not vote, and that’s the danger.” Paxton has made some headway with his intra-party opponents. In the weeks after the primary runoff, he was joined on the campaign trail by state Rep. Jeff Leach, who endorsed Cornyn in the primary and served as a leader in the 2023 impeachment case against Paxton. Yet some Texas Republicans continue to worry that GOP voters could simply skip the race. Ken Paxton’s estranged wife, Angela Paxton, addressed that possibility during a recent speech to a group of GOP women, urging them to set aside their reservations with any particular candidate for the good of the party. “When you can’t vote for, then vote against,” she said, “but vote.” For more CNN news and newsletters create an account at CNN.com This article originally appeared on CNN at https://www.cnn.com/2026/10/09/politics/ken-paxton-audio-john-cornyn

item.title: FBI arrests another ShinyHunters suspect after its own website was hacked
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The FBI's top official on Oct. 9 announced that the agency had arrested another suspected member of ShinyHunters , the digital hacking group accused of stealing personnel data from the FBI's jobs site in September. "This is the latest arrest this FBI has made in a matter of days involving this network, as we work non-stop to dismantle the group, pursue new leads and evidence, and act quickly," FBI Director Kash Patel posted on X . Patel, who did not release the identity of the person arrested, said the breach took place on a platform managed by a third-party vendor. The New York Times is reporting that the suspect is a Canadian citizen and was arrested in Pennsylvania. Officials have not said how the group − which the FBI is calling "a global cybercrime and threat actor group linked to cyberattacks in the United States, the Netherlands, and around the world" − gained access to FBIjobs.gov . But Reuters previously reported that an internal memo distributed across the FBI said officials were operating under the assumption that all current and former employees had been exposed. USA TODAY has reached out to the FBI for more information. The arrest comes on the heels of Patel, on Sept. 29, announcing that Dutch National Police had arrested one of the alleged leaders of ShinyHunters. In a statement posted on X one day earlier, Dutch police announced that they had arrested a 24-year-old man suspected of playing a role with ShinyHunters. Police also did not name that man, but Reuters reported that Benjamin Korper of Amsterdam-based cybersecurity company Neo Security said it was Pepijn van der Stap, the company's offensive security lead. Korper said Dutch investigators visited his office Sept. 15 – the same day van der Stap was arrested in a police raid that involved flash bang grenades . FBI Assistant Director Brett Leatherman said the cybercriminals have allegedly breached more than 140 organizations and taken at least $70 million in extortion payments. The group, Leatherman said, often targets "third-party vendors in cloud-based platforms, stealing sensitive data and extorting victims with threats to publish it." The case remained under investigation on Oct. 9, Patel said. Contributing: Reuters Natalie Neysa Alund is a senior reporter for USA TODAY. Reach her at nalund@usatoday.com and follow her on X @nataliealund . item.title: Obama marvels at Democrats' Senate chances
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Former president Barack Obama expressed surprise at Democrats' expanding midterm map at a private fundraiser Wednesday night, but warned donors not to get complacent about the party's chances, according to excerpts provided to The Washington Post. "There are states right now in play that I would not have imagined being in play," Obama told donors in a fireside chat in Great Falls, Virginia, with Sen. Lisa Blunt Rochester (D-Delaware), a vice chair of the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee. "If you had told me, and - I know I'm the hope guy - but if you had told me that the polling currently shows James Talarico ahead of Ken Paxton ... I would have said, eh, I don't think so." Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. Talarico, a Democratic state legislator in Texas, is leading Paxton, the state's Republican attorney general, in most public polls. Obama also mentioned competitive Senate contests in Kansas and Nebraska, as well as Sen. Jon Ossoff's large polling lead in Georgia, as other data points he wouldn't have previously believed. But Obama cautioned the crowd that winning those races is far from a sure bet. "All these races that are showing we've got a two- or three-point lead or it's a toss-up, we could end up losing all of them by two points," he said. "It's within the margin of error." The former president has been ramping up his involvement in the midterms in recent weeks, announcing an upcoming campaign stop in Michigan for Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed and cutting ads supporting candidates in crucial battlegrounds. Previously, he appeared in an ad for Iowa Senate candidate Josh Turek and at an event for Talarico. The fundraiser for the Senate Democrats' campaign arm raised $3.6 million. Republican groups hold a pronounced cash advantage over Democratic ones, driven by Trump-aligned super PAC MAGA Inc. Obama painted a bleak picture of the state of the country and emphasized the urgency of the political moment to the donors, saying he sees a threat to democracy if the Trump administration continues on its path unchecked. He criticized the Supreme Court's failure to "hold the line" against the Trump administration and stressed the importance of a Democratic Senate to the judiciary, given federal judicial nominees require Senate approval. "If you get two more years of Trump acting with impunity, along with additional judicial appointments, so that at some point the scales may tip in the direction where he's got carte blanche, you now have a very serious danger to democracy in addition to just bad policy," Obama said. If Democrats control the Senate, it could make "an enormous difference" on who is appointed, Obama said. "I would say that the judiciary, during this moment of challenge to our democracy, has bent but not broken," Obama said. "We have seen it hold the line in some important areas. To the extent it has not, it's been the Supreme Court." Obama described a "breakdown in trust, the coarsening of the public discourse, the constant violation of norms, the way that our basic institutions, the executive branch, Congress, the courts seem to have been corrupted," as signs the country is on the wrong track. "If we found out our kids were doing some of this stuff, they would be on some serious punishment, right?" Obama said of public officials' behavior. "And so, we all get a sense of a lowering of standards of behavior that extend beyond any particular policy." Obama praised Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-New York) for recruiting candidates whom he described as representative of their states and cultures, mentioning Turek's focus on tariffs and Alaska Democratic candidate Mary Peltola being "all about fish." "Being the head of the Democratic Party is a pain in the butt, because you've got people from every walk of life," Obama said. He said it can be challenging to fashion a cohesive Democratic message with such disparate candidates, but that Democrats are united by core values shared by them all. "What I can say is that I expect Democrats to stand for treating everybody with dignity and respect," he said. Obama also listed fairness for people of different sexual orientations, equal rights between men and women, ensuring an economy that is not "rigged," and believing the government should provide every child a good education among other core values. "It's not that we don't have a North Star, but we have to be able to give our candidates the ability to tailor those core values into ways that speak and relate to the particularities of the state they're in," Obama said. "I think we're doing an excellent job." ( XYZ ), are issuing payments in October as part of a settlement of a class action lawsuit over alleged security breaches that occurred between Aug. 23, 2018, and Aug. 20, 2024. The deadline to file a claim has passed. The $15 million settlement fund pays previously approved claimants up to $2,500 for out-of-pocket losses, transaction losses, and up to $75 for three hours of lost time. The other settlement, totaling $175 million, involved a consent order in which the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau accused Cash App of failing to protect users from fraud. What the Cash App settlement is about The lawsuit alleged that a former Cash App employee and an unauthorized person used recycled phone numbers to gain access to accounts. The plaintiffs also claimed that a security breach exposed personal information of Cash App Investing customers. The class action lawsuit alleged that the company failed to respond effectively to complaints about payment issues and that users found it difficult to obtain assistance from Cash App support. The company pledged to improve data security but denied any fault or wrongdoing. Read more: Do you have to pay taxes on Cash App transactions? Here's what the IRS says. Who is being paid? The deadline to file a claim was Nov. 18, 2024, and a California court gave final approval to the settlement in March 2025. Approved claimants are expected to receive payments this month by check, prepaid card, Venmo, or Zelle. About 40,380 claims were approved out of over 667,000 filed, totaling $5.6 million and averaging approximately $139 per payout, before any adjustments. Read more: Just received a settlement? For questions related to this settlement, call 888-832-1301 between 8:30 a.m. and 9:00 p.m. ET. A third settlement, a $12.5 million case over Cash App referral texts, was paid to Washington state residents in April 2026. Any offer to file a late claim or offer a Cash App payment for a fee in any settlement is likely a scam. item.title: 'It was quid pro quo': Businessman says Guilfoyle offered political access for $100,000
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Businessman Eric Deters said he has "no doubt it was pay to play," claiming Kimberly Guilfoyle, now the U.S. ambassador to Greece and ex-fiancee of Donald Trump Jr., asked him to wire $100,000 to pay her American Express bill in exchange for her help with the Trump administration ahead of Guilfoyle's Senate confirmation hearing. In an interview with CBS News, Deters said Guilfoyle should "lose her ambassadorship" over her alleged behavior, after texts between the two of them from last July were published in the Wall Street Journal . "It was quid pro quo," Deters told CBS News White House correspondent Weijia Jiang Thursday. Deters said he never gave her the money. "Unfortunately for Kimberly Guilfoyle, at that time, at that moment in time, I didn't have $100,000 to spare to give to Kimberly Guilfoyle, or I actually would have been a dumbass enough to do it." Deters said he made up an "excuse" that his wife wouldn't go along with it. White House officials were told that the text messages between Guilfoyle and Deters were authentic, sources familiar with the matter told CBS News. Some Trump aides expressed displeasure about Guilfoyle's actions, they said. The Wall Street Journal first reported this week that Guilfoyle allegedly reached out to Deters days before her congressional hearing to become a U.S. ambassador, saying she needed $100,000 to pay off her American Express credit debt in a way that wouldn't be publicly visible. "It won't show up anywhere if you wire money to American Express that's all that will show," Guilfoyle wrote to Deters on July 3, according to screen shots of texts provided to CBS News. "I have been officially announced honey please I need you to get this done for me today," she wrote, punctuating the message with a prayer-hands emoji. Her confirmation hearing took place on July 9. She sent him "American Express Instructions" in a PDF document. CBS News has reviewed the texts, which were provided by Deters as part of a 292-page file that included dozens of pages of grievances against Trump world figures, communications with Guilfoyle and others, photos of Deters with Guilfoyle, President Trump, Eric Trump and Trump Jr., and a lengthy excerpt of a book Deters has written. CBS News has reached out to spokespeople for the State Department and the White House, as well as Guilfoyle. Deters, a longtime Trump supporter, is a retired lawyer and businessman from Kentucky who was sanctioned by the Ohio Supreme Court in 2021 for engaging in the unauthorized practice of law. He has also run unsuccessfully for Kentucky governor and for Rep. Thomas Massie's U.S. House seat. For years, Deters has been trying to attract media attention and political support for a push to extradite orthopedic spine surgeon Dr. Abubakar Durrani . The government believes Durrani fled the country while he was awaiting trial for healthcare fraud charges. He was accused of billing Medicare, Medicaid and private insurance companies millions of dollars for unnecessary spinal surgeries that were potentially harmful to patients. Today, Deters said he feels slighted that he never received support for his push to have Durrani extradited to the U.S. from influential Trump world figures. "I sent Susie Wiles, Don Jr. and Kimberly Guilfoyle an email, and I told them, I said, 'You got until 5 o'clock on Monday to help me out with the Durrani victims,'" he said. "They didn't respond. And I told them, 'If you don't, I'm going to go to the media and try to get the media's help because you're not helping.' So I gave them one last shot, and they ignored me." In the text messages reviewed by CBS News, Deters, who said he also represents hundreds of Durrani's former patients, may have believed he could benefit from Durrani's extradition to the U.S. He wrote to Trump Jr. and Guilfoyle's podcast producer, Drew Lynch, and suggested, "If anyone in Don Jr or your world has an interest in listening to a pitch on how lots of money could be made for a little money in this Durrani matter let me know." Deters, who no longer practices law, once stood to gain financially if he were able to successfully sue Durrani. Just before he took office in 2025 and soon after Guilfoyle and Trump Jr. broke off their engagement, Mr. Trump announced he planned to nominate Guilfoyle to be U.S. ambassador to Greece. But Deters said her influence has waned since her relationship with Trump Jr. ended. "There was no question that she would do anything for me," Deters said. "The problem was, she was on the outs of the Trump world." Deters claimed Guilfoyle knew there was something wrong about asking for the payment. "She knew there was something wrong about it because she kept getting mad at me," Deters said. "I mean, I'm naive, I'm putting stuff in writing, sending it to her. She's getting mad. She wants me to use Signal. I didn't know what Signal was." In late June 2025, she texted, "Eric, I really wish you would stop papering these things. It's really dangerous and not helpful to you and not helpful to you or me while you could simply just call me on Signal." Deters had just sent her a memo to complain that she had not delivered on things that he had asked of her, including getting him booked on Tucker Carlson's podcast. "I generously offered you $1 million dollars when Durrani settles if you got me on Tucker," he wrote. He also complained that he had prepared a "concise summary" for then-Attorney General Pam Bondi, but "I have not received nothing concrete." CBS News senior White House reporter Jennifer Jacobs asked: "Do you have any reaction to a U.S. government official, in this case a U.S. ambassador, asking someone to pay off debt in exchange to access to other government officials?" "With that hypothetical, obviously I don't love that, but I, you know, I don't know exactly who you're talking about. I don't know the full details," Vance responded. Deters insisted his relationship with Guilfoyle was purely political. "Kimberly Guilfoyle and I have absolutely zero personal relationship, nada," he told CBS News. "I'm a tough hombre," Deters said. "I'm going to get to take Kimberly Guilfoyle's deposition." item.title: Democrats unite around Hegseth impeachment push
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The News Congressional Democrats aren’t eager to impeach Donald Trump. Pete Hegseth is a different story. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries and his leadership circle remain reluctant to lean too far into talking about impeaching the president if they regain power next month, a move that would revive the bruising battles of Trump’s first term. But as the Iran war squeezes Republicans ahead of the midterms, Democrats are aligning to call for the defense secretary’s ouster or resignation. With impeachment still a dirty word among many House Democrats, targeting Cabinet secretaries could be a pressure release valve for lawmakers itching for action against the Trump administration. “I 100% believe Pete Hegseth needs to be impeached and removed from office, because not only is he the worst secretary of defense in American history, he is a dangerous war criminal,” said Rep. Melanie Stansbury, D-N.M., who said it should be one of the caucus’ “top three priorities” next year. Hegseth was reviled by the left even before the Iran war began, and since then he’s faced criticism from Republicans for his handling of the war. An impeachment vote could even be bipartisan: When the House returns after the midterms, it’ll be forced to take up a Hegseth ouster resolution filed by iconoclastic Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky. Prioritizing Hegseth impeachment would solve a big problem for Democrats: If they win the House, their leaders will face intense pressure from the base to show a new level of fight against Trump. Yet they’re leery of the internal divisions or appearance of overreach that a third Trump impeachment might create, and still smarting from his return to office after two impeachment votes. In public, top Democrats are accordingly circumspect on targeting Hegseth. Jeffries says Hegseth should be fired and that Democrats “haven’t ruled anything out” in their investigations. Democrats have filed impeachment articles against other Trump Cabinet officials, like Education Secretary Linda McMahon and Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. Rep. Yassamin Ansari, D-Ariz., has also filed impeachment articles against Hegseth. Yet interviews with a half dozen Democrats pointed to Hegseth as the safest place to land. It’s not just safe-seat Democrats willing to take the plunge: Rep. Kristen McDonald Rivet, D-Mich., who represents a Trump-won district, said she was open to the possibility. “If I were Pete Hegseth, I’d be worried. It’s certainly something that needs serious consideration, and I hear Democrats, yes, but I also hear some Republicans saying it as well. I think there’s a lot he needs to answer for,” she said. Of course, it may not be even up to Democratic leaders in the end. Impeachment politics next year could be driven by an incoming crop of progressive lawmakers who could form a sizable bloc in the caucus. Any member can force a vote on an impeachment resolution, which outgoing Rep. Al Green, D-Texas, repeatedly triggered during Trump’s first term and his current one. “Pete Hegseth should be impeached. Congress never voted for a war with Iran, and he’s been running one since February anyway. It’s cost innocent lives and more than $40 billion of our money,” said Melat Kiros, a Colorado progressive who is heavily favored to win election to the House in November. Massie’s Hegseth resolution, among other allegations, lays out charges of violating Congress’ war powers and carrying out extrajudicial killings. “They all should be impeached — President Trump and his cabinet that’s enabled him to do everything that he has right now,” said Adam Hamawy, a fellow Justice Democrats-aligned progressive from New Jersey. “Now, whether we’re going to be able to do that is another thing, but it’s not something that, you know, we should just ignore because it’s not possible.” The Pentagon defended Hegseth’s record in a statement. “Secretary Hegseth has slashed bureaucracy, unleashed innovation, and delivered for our warfighters every step of the way,” said Pentagon press secretary Kingsley Wilson, adding that the Pentagon “is better under President Trump and Secretary Hegseth’s leadership than before.” Know More It’s unclear if Hegseth will leave the administration post-midterms. While Trump is known to be unpredictable, he likes Hegseth a lot, and those familiar with the situation are skeptical of any looming changes at the top of the department. Still, other Democrats say they need to balance impeachment with acting on cost-of-living issues like healthcare that they believe will tip the midterms in their favor. “There’s going to have to be a balance of addressing needs and meeting our constituents where they’re at, and also part of restoring the faith of the American people in our own government and restoring the integrity of our democratic institutions — it requires holding bad actors to justice,” said Rep. Analilia Mejia, D-N.J. The Massie resolution will be a good test for Democratic support for going after Hegseth. Some Democrats are loath to support a measure drafted by a Republican and before any kind of investigative process has been completed. But some leaders like Rep. Adam Smith, D-Wash., the top Armed Services Committee Democrat, have signaled they could back the Massie measure. The House has only ever impeached two Cabinet secretaries, with the most recent being the GOP-led impeachment of Homeland Security Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas in 2024. The then-Democratic Senate voted to toss the articles of impeachment. If Democrats take both the House and Senate next year, Hegseth could get a debilitating trial in the upper chamber. Nicholas’s view Taking on Hegseth is basically a free shot for Democrats. It allows them to demonstrate to the base that they could take action against the Trump administration without the risk of backlash that impeaching the president himself could bring. But they’ll only be able to keep a lid on the prospect of impeaching Trump for so long. With many in the party pushing for investigations of potential malfeasance by the administration, party leaders will face tough choices about consequences if those probes do turn up wrongdoing. And unlike 2018, when purple-district Democrats ran away from impeaching Trump, some are already embracing it. San Diego City Councilmember Marni von Wilpert, who’s running in a newly redrawn purple district, called recent comments by Trump about Iran’s ability to “take out” San Diego and Los Angeles an “impeachable offense.” Notable Democrats on the House Armed Services Committee are weighing the creation of an oversight subpanel to probe Hegseth’s department, Politico reported. item.title: Vance casts doubt on Pentagon plan to livestream Fort Hood shooter's execution
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
HEBRON, Ky. (AP) — Vice President JD Vance cast doubt Friday on whether the Pentagon will livestream the execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Malik Hasan in December but told reporters that if it is livestreamed, “I’m not going to be watching it.” The Republican vice president said, “I don’t know that that’s actually going to happen,” when asked about the plans that the Pentagon confirmed Thursday. But Vance then tried to set aside the controversy over the shocking plans for a public execution and said Hasan’s crimes should not be forgotten. Hasan was convicted of killing 13 people and injuring 32 others in a shooting spree at the military base in 2009. “So whatever the controversy is about the method of the execution, I hope that people don’t forget that this is a guy who brutally murdered a lot of innocent people,” Vance said. “Now, that said, I mean, look, if it’s ultimately livestreamed, I’m not going to be watching it,” he added. Vance is a convert to the Catholic Church, which has long opposed capital punishment. Earlier Friday morning, the head of the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops condemned the U.S. government’s decision to livestream Hasan's execution. “It is with shock and great sorrow that I have learned of the Department of War’s decision to publicly livestream the execution,” Archbishop Paul S. Coakley, president of the conference, said in a statement. He added that the decision was “a barbaric promotion of a culture of death and must be reconsidered.” Earlier, President Donald Trump told a White House event that Hasan will be getting “the death penalty through firing squad. And he deserves it.” Trump, who approved Hasan's execution, called him “a maniac.” The president approved the method of execution by firing squad days after a failed attempt to execute Christa Pike by lethal injection late last month pushed Tennessee’s governor to halt further executions in that state this year. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said the military hasn’t executed a service member by firing squad since World War II. The last military execution took place on April 13, 1961, when Army Pvt. John Bennett was executed by hanging. Trump, who has long been a vocal supporter of capital punishment, didn’t mention the plans that the Pentagon has announced to livestream the execution so that the broader public can see it. ___ This story has been corrected to show the military base's name is Fort Hood, not Ford Hood. ___ Associated Press writers Will Weissert in Washington and Holly Meyer in Nashville, Tennessee contributed to this report.
